strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel attack scenario: an input-aware backdoor for VLM visual grounding, where a text-conditional U-Net embeds the semantic description of an attacker-chosen target object into the image, forcing the model to ground that target regardless of the user query. This differs meaningfully from prior fixed-pattern or prompt-level backdoors (TrojVLM, BadEncoder) and addresses the open-vocabulary nature of grounding.

The method is technically coherent: the text-conditioned U-Net trigger generator, the smoothed L1 reconstruction loss for stealth, and the joint clean/poisoned LM loss are well-motivated and clearly described, with an overall framework figure and algorithm listing aiding reproducibility.

Empirical evaluation is broad: three victim VLMs (InternVL-2.5-8B, LLaVA-1.5-7B, Ferret-7B) across four datasets (RefCoco, RefCoco+, RefCocog, Coco-2017), with ASR@0.5 reaching ~66.7% on InternVL and ~55% on LLaVA, plus clean-accuracy retention that is largely preserved.

Supporting analyses go beyond the headline result: ablations (trigger-only, w/o L_rec, w/o L_LM, w/o joint training), transferability across datasets, poison-rate sensitivity (including 0.01), inference-time overhead, and real-world/GUI visualizations. These strengthen the claim that the attack is practical and stealthy.

The attack is shown to survive three representative defenses (Spectral Signature, Beatrix, PAR) with nearly unchanged ASR, which is a useful (if limited) signal about the difficulty of defending input-aware triggers.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Proposition 1, Lemmas 1-4) is largely vacuous padding: existence follows from universal approximation of U-Net/ViT, and convergence follows from standard smoothness + Polyak-Lojasiewicz conditions. These are generic properties of over-parameterized networks and do not provide meaningful guarantees specific to the proposed attack or its optimization; the section adds length without adding insight.

Defense evaluation is thin and not convincing. Only three defenses are tested, none of which is designed for input-aware/adaptive triggers, and the paper itself concedes no such defenses exist. A backdoor paper's practical threat hinges on resisting defense, so the claim of robustness would be far stronger with trigger-inversion methods (e.g., Neural Cleanse-style), input-aware detection, or fine-tuning/repair defenses.

The comparison to prior attacks in Table 2 is conducted in a deliberately simplified 'close-vocabulary, 100-target-object' setting, which the authors acknowledge is not the same task. This makes the 'beat previous SOTA' framing somewhat unfair to the baselines and weakens the empirical comparison.

There is a discrepancy between the claimed '1%-3% clean accuracy decrease' and the reported numbers: on InternVL-2.5-8B, CA@0.5 on RefCoco val is 94.5 while BA@0.5 is 89.5, a ~5-point drop; on RefCoco+ val the drop is also ~4 points. The stealth claim should be stated more accurately.

The threat model requires white-box access to training data and full control of the fine-tuning process (supply-chain assumption). While standard for backdoor work, the paper does not quantify how sensitive the attack is to partial access (e.g., unknown architecture, limited poisoning budget at very low rates beyond the single curve in Fig. 4) or to which layers/adapters are frozen.

ASR on Ferret-7B hovers near 50% and on several settings is only marginally above the random/shortcut level, so the attack is not uniformly strong; the paper's discussion attributes this to open-vocabulary/generation difficulty but does not analyze failure cases quantitatively.

Several presentation issues: equations are inconsistently numbered (e.g., repeated '(0)', '(2)'), internal cross-references are garbled (e.g., 'Equation (A.1)' vs 'Step 1'), and the appendix numbering of figures/tables is hard to follow. These do not undermine the science but reduce clarity.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes an underexplored security threat: an input-aware backdoor attack on VLM visual grounding, with a realistic supply-chain threat model and practical downstream implications.

Proposes a technically coherent adaptive trigger generator using a text-conditional U-Net, conditioning on the attacker-targeted object description and adding a reconstruction loss to encourage stealth.

Provides a unified poisoned-data generation pipeline and evaluates across multiple VLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B, InternVL-2.5-8B, Ferret-7B) and grounding datasets, showing meaningful attack success while maintaining clean accuracy.
Includes a reasonably broad empirical study with ablations, poison-rate curves, cross-dataset transferability, inference-time analysis, defense evaluation, and real-world qualitative visualizations.
Reproducibility is supported by algorithm pseudocode, detailed hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and a stated plan to release code/datasets.
The paper is generally well organized and the case studies/visualizations effectively communicate the stealth and potential risks of the attack.
weaknesses: The theoretical 'existence' result relies on strong, near-circular assumptions, including universal approximation of the victim/generator and the existence of a fixed trigger pattern sufficient to uniquely activate the target language; it does not rigorously establish the claimed open-vocabulary, input-aware guarantee.

The convergence analysis is sketched rather than fully rigorous: the sum of cross-entropy and smoothed L1 losses is asserted to satisfy Polyak-Lojasiewicz conditions without adequately addressing nonconvexity or conflicting clean/poisoned objectives.

Baseline comparison is limited and potentially unfair: BadEncoder and TrojVLM are not designed for visual grounding/generative VLMs, and BadSem is discussed but not empirically compared, so superiority over prior backdoor attacks is not fully substantiated.
The ablation study does not quantitatively isolate the contribution of the reconstruction loss, even though stealth is a central claim; the evidence for L_rec is mainly qualitative.
Defense evaluation is narrow and lacks implementation details (e.g., how defenses are trained/applied, hyperparameters, clean-data budgets), making it difficult to assess robustness claims.
Attack success rates are moderate on some datasets (e.g., around 40-50% ASR@0.5), and the paper does not fully analyze failure modes or whether stronger poisoning is practical.

There are presentation inconsistencies: the poison-rate text mentions 0.01 while the figure/experiments discuss 1/5/10%, 'mix-up' terminology is non-standard, and the IoU definition is imprecisely worded.
For an attack paper, there is no broader-impact or responsible-disclosure discussion, which would strengthen the work's framing and usefulness to the community.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored and timely security problem: backdoor attacks on VLM visual grounding, where models may be manipulated to ground an attacker-specified target regardless of the user query.

Proposes an input-aware adaptive trigger generator using a text-conditional U-Net conditioned on the target object's description, which is more flexible than fixed-trigger backdoor attacks and can generate triggers for open-vocabulary target objects.

Uses a reconstruction loss to encourage imperceptibility and a language-model loss on both clean and poisoned samples to preserve clean-input performance, with a joint training procedure that ablations show is important.

Evaluates across three VLM families (LLaVA-v1.5-7B, InternVL-2.5-8B, Ferret-7B) and multiple grounding datasets (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, Coco-2017), reporting ASR, benign accuracy, and clean accuracy.

Includes additional studies on poison rate, attack transferability, potential defenses, time consumption, and real-world visualizations, which together provide a broad empirical picture of the attack's behavior.
Provides an algorithm box and hyperparameter table, and promises code/dataset release, indicating some attention to reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is not sound for the stated threat model. Proposition 1 assumes a modified victim model with an explicit gate p(I) and a two-branch composition F_phi(I) = (1-p(I)) LM_clean(I) + p(I) B_t, but the threat model states the attacker cannot modify the model architecture or inference code. The proof therefore establishes existence for an altered architecture, not for a standard VLM trained with the proposed loss, so the claimed theoretical guarantee of feasibility is largely vacuous.

The convergence proof relies on strong assumptions (smoothness, Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, separable data, over-parameterization) and does not establish that optimization finds a model that actually satisfies the backdoor behavior; it only shows convergence to a stationary/global optimum under those assumptions.

The central ASR metric lacks an essential control: the paper never reports how often a clean (non-backdoored) model grounds the attack-target object when given the same poisoned images and unrelated queries. Without this baseline, the reported 50-70% ASR could be partially explained by target-object saliency, query ambiguity, or dataset biases rather than the trigger's effect.

The stealthiness claim is not quantitatively supported. There is no PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, or detection-rate evaluation of the poisoned images, nor a user study. The reconstruction loss is only a training objective, not a hard imperceptibility guarantee, and the visual examples are too small to verify that triggers are imperceptible.

Defense evaluation is limited to Spectral Signature, Beatrix, and PAR, which are adapted from classification/encoder backdoor defenses. There is no evaluation against trigger inversion, input preprocessing (e.g., JPEG, blur), fine-pruning, or VLM-specific defenses, making the robustness claim incomplete.

The baseline comparison is weakened by simplifying BadEncoder and TrojVLM into a close-vocabulary, 100-target-object setting that does not reflect their original design. The large reported gap may therefore overstate IAG's advantage relative to stronger, more fairly adapted backdoor baselines.

Important method details are missing or unclear: the specific U-Net architecture, the identity of the frozen language encoder used for z_O, how cross-attention conditioning is implemented, the meaning and implementation of 'mixup,' and the exact training schedule/loss balancing. These omissions limit reproducibility.

The evaluation reports only ASR@0.5 and BA/CA at IoU 0.5, with no lower-threshold IoU results, mIoU, or variance/error bars over multiple runs. The results vary substantially across datasets (e.g., RefCocog ASR 49.0% for InternVL), and the claim of 'over 65% on various testing sets' is not uniformly supported.

The paper contains presentation issues, including broken equation numbering (multiple equations numbered (0) and (-2)), inconsistent notation, and minor reference/formatting errors, which reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper identifies a novel and timely security threat: multi-target backdoor attacks on VLM-based visual grounding, moving beyond static triggers and fixed targets of prior VLM backdoor work.

The proposed IAG method is technically reasonable: a text-conditioned UNet generates input-aware triggers from target-object descriptions, and a joint objective combines language modeling with pixel/LPIPS reconstruction to balance attack effectiveness and imperceptibility.

Evaluation is broad, covering three VLMs (LLaVA-v1.5-7B, InternVL-2.5-8B, Ferret-7B) and five grounding datasets (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, Flickr30k Entities, ShowUI) with ASR@0.5, benign accuracy, and clean accuracy metrics.
IAG achieves the highest ASR in 11 of 12 main settings, with large gains (e.g., 11.9%-32.8% on Flickr30k Entities and >33% on ShowUI), while clean accuracy is maintained within roughly 3%.

Robustness is examined against detection-based defenses (Spectral Signature, Beatrix) and adaptive defenses (mean/median filtering, JPEG compression, re-training, quantization, PAR), showing the attack largely persists and is difficult to mitigate with off-the-shelf defenses.

Additional analyses strengthen the paper: unnoticeability metrics, poison-rate sensitivity (1%, 5%, 10%), time overhead, dataset transferability, VQA transfer, real-world examples, ablations, and a theoretical margin lower bound.

The supplementary material provides useful reproducibility details, including algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameters, generator architecture, dataset statistics, baseline reproduction, defense implementation, and ethical discussion.
weaknesses: The threat model requires both a poisoned VLM and an external trigger generator at inference; the backdoored model alone cannot be triggered without the attacker's generator, which is closer to test-time adversarial manipulation than to a classic backdoor and needs stronger practical justification.

Technical novelty is moderate: the approach combines existing input-aware backdoor ideas, text-conditioned UNet design, and LoRA fine-tuning in a new task, rather than introducing fundamentally new attack mechanisms.

Direct VLM visual-grounding backdoor baselines are limited; the strongest static VLM backdoors are compared only in supplementary Table 10, while the main baselines are adapted from image-classification tasks, which may not fully represent the state of the art.

Defense evaluation, while useful, does not include several standard backdoor mitigation techniques (e.g., fine-pruning, neural cleanse, stronger clean fine-tuning) and relies on supplementary details for re-training/quantization, leaving the robustness claims not fully exhaustive.

Main results lack variance or standard deviation over multiple random seeds, so the reported ASR and clean-accuracy numbers may be sensitive to initialization, data ordering, or hyperparameter choices.

Unnoticeability is supported only by automated metrics (PSNR ~31-32 dB, LPIPS ~0.03); PSNR at this level can be perceptible in smooth regions, and no human study or user study is provided to validate stealthiness.

The theoretical analysis depends on assumptions A1-A3 that are not empirically validated and on constants (m, C, gamma) that are not estimated, so Proposition 1 provides intuition rather than a strong practical guarantee.

The abstract's claim of 'any specified target object description' is slightly broader than the evaluated setting, where targets are objects present in the image; absent-object targets are not demonstrated. Additionally, 'transferability across models' is not directly tested via cross-model trigger transfer.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a novel and realistic security threat: a multi-target backdoor attack against VLM-based visual grounding, extending backdoor attacks beyond static triggers and fixed target classes.

The proposed IAG method is technically well-motivated: it uses an input-aware, text-conditioned UNet to generate dynamic triggers that embed target-specific semantic cues while a joint loss balances language supervision and perceptual reconstruction for stealthiness.

The experimental evaluation is broad and convincing: three VLMs (LLaVA-v1.5-7B, InternVL-2.5-8B, Ferret-7B), multiple grounding datasets (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCocog, Flickr30k Entities, ShowUI), and 12 settings show IAG achieving the highest ASR in 11/12 cases while maintaining clean accuracy within 3%.

The paper provides useful analyses: ablations validate the trigger generator and joint training, poison-rate curves show effectiveness even at 1%, transferability across datasets/tasks is demonstrated, and real-world GUI/screenshot cases illustrate practical risk.

Defense evaluations are relatively thorough for the VLM backdoor setting, including Spectral Signature, Beatrix, filtering, JPEG compression, re-training, quantization, and PAR; the results suggest existing defenses are largely ineffective against IAG.

Presentation is clear, with a well-organized main paper and a comprehensive supplementary containing architecture details, proofs, attack data examples, hyperparameters, algorithm, and ethical considerations.
The work has strong potential usefulness for the trustworthy multimodal community by exposing an overlooked vulnerability and motivating future defenses for grounding-capable VLMs.
weaknesses: The threat model assumes the attacker can append a generated trigger to the victim's input at inference time (e.g., via a malicious webpage or screenshot). This is plausible in some GUI/agent scenarios, but the paper does not fully analyze how broadly this applies to other real-world visual grounding deployments, limiting the practical scope.

The evaluation only considers attack targets that are actually present in the image and selected from annotations; there is no analysis of failure cases, absent targets, or truly arbitrary open-world target descriptions. The claimed 'any object' generality is therefore not fully stress-tested.

Several baselines are adapted from classification backdoor attacks and some are very weak (One-to-N, Random); although Imperio and Marksman are more relevant, the comparison would be stronger with additional adaptive or grounding-specific attacks and with baselines tuned specifically for visual grounding.

The defense suite, while useful, omits several standard backdoor defenses (e.g., Neural Cleanse, STRIP, fine-pruning, ABL) and does not include an adaptive defense that knows the trigger generator; robustness claims against 'existing defenses' are therefore somewhat narrower than stated.

The theoretical Proposition 1 relies on strong, unverified assumptions (A1–A3) about the perceptual subspace, local linearization, and target-aligned feature shift. It provides intuition but is not a rigorous guarantee and may overstate the formal grounding of the method.

The main results are point estimates without variance or multiple seeds, so small differences (e.g., a few ASR points) may not be statistically significant; this is especially relevant when claiming superiority in 11/12 settings.

The method's components—UNet trigger generator, text conditioning, LPIPS reconstruction, and joint LM loss—are adapted from existing input-aware backdoor techniques. The novelty is primarily in the new task/domain rather than in fundamentally new methodology, which somewhat limits the technical contribution.

The VQA hate-speech extension is ethically sensitive and tangential to the core visual grounding contribution; despite the warning and ethical section, it may raise concerns and distract from the main message.
The paper lacks a dedicated limitations section and does not mention a code release, which slightly weakens reproducibility and transparency despite the otherwise detailed supplementary material.

strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant security problem: the paper exposes that VLM-based visual grounding can be hijacked by backdoors, with concrete implications for GUI agents and embodied AI (Figure 1, Case 1 in the supplement).

Experimental coverage is broad: three VLMs (LLaVA-v1.5-7B, InternVL-2.5-8B, Ferret-7B) across five grounding benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, F30k Entities, ShowUI), plus transferability studies to VQA/OKVQA and benign-benchmark checks (Tables 1, 8, 11, 12, 13).

The stealthiness/effectiveness trade-off is handled reasonably: the reconstruction loss (L1 + LPIPS) keeps PSNR at ~31-32 dB and LPIPS ~0.03 while benign accuracy stays within ~3% of clean accuracy (Tables 1, 2).
The supplementary is unusually thorough (architecture, assumptions/proofs, hyperparameters, defense details, real-world examples, attention visualization), which aids reproducibility.
The attack is demonstrated in genuinely realistic scenarios (webpages, GUI buttons, real photographs in Figures 7-12), making the vulnerability tangible rather than purely synthetic.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core mechanism—a generator conditioned on the target's text embedding that produces an input-aware trigger—is essentially the input-aware backdoor idea from Imperio/Marksman (which the paper itself cites and uses as baselines), ported to VLM grounding with a UNet in place of an MLP. The 'multi-target' framing is the main new element, but it is a direct consequence of conditioning on text embeddings rather than a new attack principle.

Empirical gains over adapted baselines are modest and not always favorable. On RefCoco/LLaVA IAG gets 58.9 vs Imperio 55.2, but on RefCocog/InternVL Imperio actually beats IAG (52.4 vs 50.2). No variance, seeds, or significance tests are reported, so the 'highest ASR in 11/12 settings' claim is hard to assess rigorously.

The theoretical analysis is largely circular. Proposition 1 relies on assumptions A1-A3, and A3 explicitly posits that the trigger-induced feature shift aligns with the margin gradient with high probability—i.e., it essentially assumes the attack succeeds. The Taylor-expansion 'proof' therefore does not provide independent insight into when the attack works.

The defense evaluation is unconvincing and over-claimed. Several evaluated defenses (Spectral Signature, Beatrix, mean/median filtering, quantization) are not designed for this threat, and 'Re-train' is not specified in the main text (only 'Appendix K'). Concluding that 'existing defenses fail' from this mix is a strong claim that is not adequately supported; a defense-aware or poisoning-rate-aware evaluation is missing.

The central 'input-aware' framing is weakened by the paper's own ablation: a trigger-only variant still achieves 63.0 ASR vs 66.9 for the full model (Table 3), i.e., input-awareness contributes only ~4 points. This suggests the trigger largely encodes target semantics on its own, undercutting the motivation for the UNet-based image-conditioned design.

Threat-model and generality gaps: the target object must be present in the image, and the attacker must pre-craft triggered images with the generator; the paper never evaluates generalization to target categories unseen during training, which is the crux of the 'any object' claim.

Imperceptibility is argued only via PSNR/LPIPS; ~32 dB can still be visible on text-heavy UI/webpage images (the very setting the paper emphasizes), and no human study or detection-rate analysis is provided.
